description: "The cluster Devs", un equipo de estudiantes de Ingeniería en Desarrollo de Software apasionados por crear aplicaciones funcionales basadas en datos. Nuestro núcleo técnico incluye Python, Machine Learning (TensorFlow, Scikit-learn), Visión por Computadora (OpenCV) y arquitectura robusta de bases de datos (SQL).
summary: Martian Map is a web app that helps a crew on Mars plan a safe surface walk (EVA) around their landing site, built on real NASA data for Jezero and Gale craters. It guides the crew in five steps: choose a site on a global Mars map, land the habitat only on terrain that meets NASA landing rules, plan a route through real science targets studied by Perseverance and Curiosity, review a GO/NO-GO checklist for slope, oxygen and radiation, and walk the route in a first-person helmet view. It turns orbital elevation, imagery, geology, AI crater detection and rover data into one map a crew can trust: where it is safe to land, where it is safe to walk, and what is worth studying. Safety rules use real values, such as Mars Science Laboratory slope limits and the solar storm Curiosity measured on 20 May 2024. It works offline in any browser.
details:
Martian Map plans a safe, science-driven walk (EVA) for a crew on Mars, from choosing the landing site to walking the route. It covers a 6 km by 6 km zone in Jezero Crater and one in Gale Crater.

WHAT IT DOES: FIVE MISSION STEPS

1. Mars: a global color map of Mars (works offline) shows past landing sites. The crew picks Jezero or Gale.

2. Land: every 10 m of the site is graded safe, caution or no-landing. The habitat cannot be placed on a red cell, and the app can suggest the three safest spots.

3. Plan: the crew chooses science objectives. Each star on the map is a real place studied by Perseverance or Curiosity, with what to study, which instrument to use, whether to take a sample, the sol the rover was there, a NASA source and real rover photos. One button adds the selected targets to the route, nearest first.

4. Review: a 3D model of the terrain shows the route. A checklist gives GO or NO-GO for landing spot, slope, craters, oxygen, radiation dose and science objectives covered.

5. Execute: a first-person helmet view walks the route with distance, oxygen, dose and the photo of each science stop.

HOW IT WORKS

- Terrain: we build a 2 m elevation grid from NASA HiRISE and CTX digital terrain models, then compute slope and surface roughness.

- Landing safety: we apply the engineering limits used for the Mars Science Laboratory landing (slope of 15 degrees or less), plus craters, sand dunes from the USGS geologic map and a 50 m clear radius.

- Craters: a YOLO model we trained detects craters on orbital photos. Each detection is checked against the elevation data: a real crater must be a depression with a rim, and detections the relief contradicts are rejected.

- Route: an A* search finds the best path between stops, with walking speed from Tobler's hiking function, avoiding steep or blocked terrain.

- Life support: oxygen use comes from walking time. Radiation uses about 0.67 mSv per day on the surface; in a solar storm the dose is multiplied by 11.6, the jump Curiosity's RAD detector measured on 20 May 2024 (8,100 microgray in one day vs. about 700 on a normal day).

- Science: each science place is positioned where the rover was on the sol it studied that target, from NASA's rover traverse data. Rover photos come from NASA's public raw image archives and are stored inside the app.

- Offline and bilingual: a service worker stores the app, data and photos, so it works with no server or internet. All text is in English and Spanish.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

- Perseverance's real landing point falls on a safe cell of our landing map; 38.4% of the Jezero zone is graded safe.

- 99.8% of Perseverance's real path is walkable under our slope rules.

- Compared with Perseverance's path (24 legs of 800 m), our route is on average 43 m away, and 69% of it lies within 50 m of the rover's path.

- Crater detection: 2,676 YOLO detections checked against relief; 18 confirmed, 119 rejected, the rest too small or shallow to confirm; 779 shown at 50% confidence or more.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

A crew gets one map that answers three questions at once: where it is safe to land, where it is safe to walk, and what is worth studying. The app refuses unsafe choices instead of only warning about them, and every number shows its source, so mission planners can trust it or change it.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It joins orbital data, AI crater detection and real rover history in one mission flow, and it tests its own decisions against what Perseverance actually did on Mars. It also turns a real solar storm into a GO/NO-GO decision the crew can see.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Astronaut safety first (slope, oxygen, radiation, a walk-back reserve), science value of every stop, honesty about which values are real and which are assumptions, and use in the field: offline, any browser, touch screens and two languages.

GOALS

Add more sites with the same pipeline, thermal and mineral layers (THEMIS, CRISM), live space weather, team or rover-assisted walks, and the same planner for walks on the Moon.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

JavaScript, HTML, CSS and Python. Leaflet for 2D maps, Three.js for the 3D terrain and helmet view, a service worker for offline use, hosted on GitHub Pages. Data pipeline in Python with NumPy, Pillow, OpenCV, Ultralytics YOLO and requests, plus Node.js scripts for route validation. Git and GitHub for teamwork.

Live app: https://marshvidlex.github.io/martian-map-hackathon/
